newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW-Scotia - three new drugs by 1998.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Scotia - three new drugs by 1998.

text.p: By Neil Winton, Science and Technology Correspondent
Nutritional products and pharmaceuticals maker Scotia Holdings expects to have three new drugs licensed and on sale by 1998.

Scotia said the drugs -- Tarabetic (EF4) which combats the side effects of diabetes, EF 13 to treat pancreatic cancer, and EF27 which prevents side effects from cancer radiotherapy -- should all be approved within about two years.

"I can't say when they will be approved but I think there is a chance of two of them being approved at the end of this year and 1997, and the third by 1998. Certainly by the end of 1998 I think we will get all of them approved," chief executive Dr David Horrobin said in an interview.

Scotia, which was floated on the London Stock Exchange in October 1993 and has annual sales of about 16 million, is due to announce its half year results on Tuesday, when half year pre-tax losses are expected to widen to around eight million pounds ($12.5 million).
Horrobin said a fourth drug Foscan, used in photodynamic therapy, should also be available by 1998.
"We would expect approval within the next two years. This (Foscan) would be the fourth drug, and would probably be the most important single drug we have got," Horrobin said.

Photodynamic therapy uses lasers to attack cancer tumours which were previously inaccessible. Foscan is injected into the patient and accumulates in the target tumors. Lasers then activate the drug which kills the cancer cells.

Horrobin was talking in his office overlooking East Loch Roag at the company's new plant about 20 miles west of Stornoway, in the outer Hebrides, a few hundred yards from the 4000-year-old Standing Stones of Callanish.
It opened a new six million pound research and production facility there last week.
But why operate in such a remote location? "We are actually here for practical reasons. We had a deal with a local fish oil company because we used this in our products," Horrobin said.

"But I do quite deliberately like to site places away from major cities. We are in Nova Scotia (Canada), Carlisle (north west England), the south of Sweden and here. The kind of staff we want like these places."
As well as pharmaceuticals, Scotia makes nutritional products based on the seed oil of the evening primrose, and lithium.
"The split is roughly 50-50 at the moment, and in fact both are beginning to grow quite strongly although potential for the pharmaceuticals side is very much larger than for the OTC side."
"By the end of the century I'd expect the ratio to change to 70 to 80 percent pharamaceutical, 20 to 30 percent nutritional."
Horrobin has high hopes for the drugs nearing licensing.

"The diabetes drug treats side effects, in particular nerve damage. That's important because that's the main cause of foot ulceration and amputation in diabetes. There are roughly 6,000 amputations in Britain each year because of diabetes and 30,000 in the States."

"Pancreatic cancer is about 30,000 cases a year in Europe. It is currently untreatable really. The average survival is only about three months after diagnoses, by far the most lethal type of cancer and we believe that this drug will more than double survival and maybe do better than that.
"We also think that it can be applied to other cancers beyond pancreatic cancer, and so this too is potentially a rather large drug."

"And the drug for preventing side effects of radiotherapy for cancer. Radiotherapy is used in about half of all patients with cancer. It often cannot cure people because you cannot give them quite enough radiation to kill the cancer cells.

"What this drug does is prevent that damage to normal tissue so you can reduce the side effects of radiation and at the same time increase the radiation dose and increase the likelihood of a cure." ($1=.6385 Pound)
